candidates.statement: In order to fully exploit this type of construction, one should ideally give an alternative explicit definition of these "effective" theories directly in $6-d$ dimensions.
The compactification of the six-dimensional theory on the cobordism should give a domain wall between the 4d theories associated to the Riemann surfaces.
This should be contrasted with a similar approach in $d=2$, where the tubes are all cylinders with $S^1$ cross-section, and the only plumbing fixture is the pair of pants.

Instead, we wish to associate a simple "building block" theory $T_{\Delta}$ to each tetrahedron $\Delta$, and to define the field theory analogue of the geometric gluing with a simple constraint in mind: different triangulations of the same manifold must give equivalent definitions of the corresponding theory, in the sense that they flow to the same SCFT in the IR.

For example, quantities like the superconformal index of $T_M$ or the partition function on $S^3$ should map to interesting three-manifold invariants, as summarized in Table [1](#tab:dict){reference-type="ref" reference="tab:dict"}.
- The moduli space of vacua of the 3d theory must coincide (with some caveats) with the space of flat $SL(2)$ connections on $M$.
- The partition function of $T[M,\mathfrak{g}]$ on an ellipsoid $S^3_b$, as in [@HHL], should coincide with the (analytically continued) $\mathfrak{g}$ Chern-Simons partition function on $M$.

Finally, we should describe in more detail the class of 3-manifolds $M$ to which our construction applies.
In particular, the manifold should have at least one defect.

Fortunately, it seems that we can always refine a given triangulation of a 3-manifold $M$ so that no hard edges are present, and then use this triangulation to construct $T_{M,\Pi}$.\ One of our central claims is that the theories $T_{M,\Pi}$ constructed here are topological invariants of a three-manifold $M$ (and a polarization of its boundary), which do not depend on the actual triangulation being used to define them --- or on the choice of refinement, should a given triangulation include hard edges.

Similarly, the space $\mathcal{M}_{\rm SUSY}^{(\rm param)}(T_{M,\Pi})$ should not depend on the polarization $\Pi$ (or boundary triangulation, etc.) used in previous sections to define a theory $T_{M,\Pi}$.

In particular, changing the polarization $\Pi$ merely shifts the duality frame of the combined 4d-3d system, and must map $\mathcal{M}_{\rm SUSY}^{(\rm param)}(T_M)$ to an isomorphic space.\ The present discussion of supersymmetric vacua, particularly as given by equations [\[uidef\]](#uidef){reference-type="eqref" reference="uidef"} with $\widetilde W$ a sum of dilogarithm functions, is highly reminiscent of recent work relating effective 2d field theories to quantum integrable systems [@NS-I; @NShatashvili; @NRS].

As we discussed in section [\[sec:S3b\]](#sec:S3b){reference-type="ref" reference="sec:S3b"}, a supersymmetric Chern-Simons interaction at level $k$ for the background gauge field contributes to the partition function a factor [\[z3dCSk\]](#z3dCSk){reference-type="eqref" reference="z3dCSk"}: $$\mathcal{Z}_{CS_k} = e^{- i \pi k \tilde m^2} \,.$$ Much like the partition function of the theory $T_{\Delta}$, it obeys the following $q$-difference equation: $$\left( \hat z'' - q^{\frac k2} \, \hat z^k \right) \mathcal{Z}_{CS_k} = \left( e^{ib \partial_{\tilde m}} - e^{i\pi b^2 k+2\pi bk\tilde m} \right) \mathcal{Z}_{CS_k} = 0 \,.$$ According to [\[whhlines\]](#whhlines){reference-type="eqref" reference="whhlines"}, this identity should be interpreted as a statement that at a 3d boundary with Chern-Simons term at level $k$ a 't Hooft operator with one unit of a magnetic flux is equivalent to a Wilson operator of electric charge $k$, $$H - e^{i\pi b^2 k} \, W^{k} \; \simeq \; 0 \,.$$ This is indeed correct, as one can easily verify by doing a direct path integral manipulation.
